phrases.translation: Alif-Lãm-Mĩm
phrases.explanation:
Alif-Lam-Mim is one of the openings made of separate letters, and the earliest exegetes differed about what it means. Some said it is one of the names of the Quran, others that these are letters with which Allah opens the Quran, others that it is a name for the surah, others that it is the greatest name of Allah, and others that it is an oath by which Allah swore, belonging to His names. Some took each letter to carry a meaning of its own, different from the meaning of its neighbour, some took them to be letters of the alphabet simply placed there, some took each letter to comprise several divergent meanings, and some said that every book has a secret and the secret of the Quran is its opening letters. One further explanation is that the surahs were opened with these letters to make the polytheists listen, since they had agreed among themselves to turn away from the Quran.

An objection is raised to the view that they are names of surahs. Several surahs begin with Alif-Lam-Mim and several with Alif-Lam-Ra, and a name only marks a thing when it distinguishes it. The answer is that names are instituted for distinction in the first place, and where two things share one name, something else is added to tell them apart. Two men both called Amr are distinguished as Amr the Tamimi and Amr the Azdi, and in the same way a reader says Alif-Lam-Mim al-Baqara and Alif-Lam-Mim Al Imran. On this reading the three letters stand in the nominative, each raised by the other, and the words that follow, This is the Book, begin a new statement of their own.

The verdict preferred here is that Allah made these letters separate instead of joining them into ordinary speech because He intended each of them to point to many meanings and not to one. A single letter can carry several meanings just as a single word can. Arabic uses one word, umma, for a community, for an era, for a devout and obedient man and for a religion, and another, din, for recompense, for reckoning, for rule and obedience and for submission. So each of these letters comprises what the exegetes said of it. They belong to the names and attributes of Allah, they open the surahs, they carry the numerical values of the letters of the alphabet, and they mark and name the surahs they stand over. One explanation alone is rejected, the claim of a philologist that the letters stand for the alphabet as a whole and so mean that these letters are the Book. It is set aside because it departs from everything reported of the Companions, the Followers and the exegetes after them, and because the one who held it contradicted himself about what raises the words This is the Book, assigning that raising once to the letters, once to a pronoun inside the verse and once to a later phrase in it.

Two further points settle the matter. If Allah had intended one of these meanings to the exclusion of the rest, the Prophet would have said so plainly, because the Book was sent down to him so that he might make clear what people differed about. His leaving the letters unexplained is itself the strongest evidence that every aspect they can carry is intended. The claim that they fall outside the Arabic language altogether is answered by the Quran's own description of itself as a clear Arabic tongue. Allah addressed the Arabs only in what they knew of their speech, and letters no creature could understand would not be clear. Allah opened some surahs with praise of Himself and some with glorification, so there is nothing impossible in opening others with an oath by these letters.

phrases.translation: This is the Book!
phrases.explanation:
The word for that is used here where a reader might expect this, and most of the early exegetes took the meaning to be simply this Book. The passage explains why both pointings are sound. Anything that has just been said and has come to an end takes on something of the absent, since it is over, while still counting as present for the person being addressed, because it was only a moment ago. A listener answering a story says both That is exactly as you said and This is as you said, without any difference of meaning. So when the letters Alif-Lam-Mim had been mentioned and their meanings set out, the words that follow point back at them as something just completed and say that this which has been made clear is the Book.

Two other readings are recorded. One takes the Book to mean the surahs sent down before al-Baqara, at Mecca and Medina, so that the sense is that what those earlier surahs comprise is the Book about which there is no doubt. The other takes it to mean the Torah and the Gospel, in which case that is plainly a report about something absent and no difficulty arises at all. The first explanation is preferred, as the one that fits the Book best.

phrases.translation: There is no doubt about it
phrases.explanation:
Doubt here is the word rayb, which comes from a verb meaning that a matter disquieted someone and made them unsure, so the phrase denies that anything in this Book unsettles the mind or leaves it uncertain. A line of poetry is quoted in which the same word carries exactly that sense.

One further point is made about how the sentence hangs together. The word for guidance that follows can be read as a fresh statement of praise, as something sharing the case of the word that, or as following the position of this phrase. Which of these is allowed depends on how the opening letters are read, and the passage argues that the reading chosen at the start has to be kept consistently rather than abandoned halfway through the verse.

phrases.translation: —a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺
phrases.explanation:
The God-fearing are those who feared Allah in two directions at once. They held back from what He forbade, and they stood by what He made obligatory, so they avoided disobedience and obeyed Him in carrying it out. The verse describes them with God-fearingness generally, without limiting it to one part of what Allah has a right to, so nobody may narrow it to a single aspect without a proof that has to be accepted. Had some restricted sense been intended, Allah would have clarified it in His Book or through His Messenger.

On that basis one narrower explanation is set aside, the claim that the God-fearing are only those who kept clear of ascribing partners to Allah and of hypocrisy. A person can do both and still be corrupt in his conduct, unless hypocrisy is itself taken to mean committing what Allah forbade and neglecting what He made obligatory, which is how some of the early scholars used the word.

phrases.translation: who believe in the unseen,
phrases.explanation:
Belief here is explained from what the word means in Arabic, which is holding something to be true. A person who holds a statement to be true is called one who gives credence to it, and one who confirms his statement by his action is called a believer in the same sense. So belief is a comprehensive term covering acknowledgment of Allah, of His books and of His messengers, together with the confirming of that acknowledgment by action. The reading preferred here follows from that: these people hold the unseen to be true in word, in conviction and in deed, and the verse does not restrict them to one of those senses, since nothing in report or in reason singles any of them out.

The unseen is everything hidden from a person of any matter, from the same root as the word for being absent. There is a difference of opinion about who the verses at the opening of this surah describe. Some took them to be the believers among the Arabs alone, others took them to be the believers among the People of the Book in particular, because the Quran told them of matters they had kept hidden and secret among themselves, and that convinced them it came from Allah. Others again took them to describe every believer with these qualities, Arab and non-Arab, of the two earlier Books and beyond them.

phrases.translation: establish prayer,
phrases.explanation:
Establishing the prayer means performing it with its limits, its obligations and everything commanded in it, in the manner prescribed, rather than leaving any of it idle. Reports gloss it as the complete performance of the bowing, the prostration, the recitation and the humble attentiveness that belongs to it, and as the prescribed prayers rather than prayer in some general sense.

The word itself means supplication in the speech of the Arabs. The prescribed prayer is thought to carry that name because the one who prays turns toward the reward of Allah and asks Him for what he needs, just as a suppliant turns toward his Lord with his request.

phrases.translation: and donate from what We have provided for them
phrases.explanation: The exegetes differed over what spending covers here, and the reading preferred is the widest one. These people discharged everything obligatory upon them in their wealth, whether the alms due on it or the support of those whose maintenance fell to them, by kinship, by ownership or otherwise. Allah described them in general terms as spending from what He provided them and praised them for it, and He did not limit that praise to one kind of expenditure, so it takes in every kind a person is praised for giving. What is spent is the good He provided them, the lawful part of their wealth, with nothing forbidden mixed into it.

phrases.translation: and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you,
phrases.explanation: These words describe belief in the whole of revelation rather than in part of it, what was sent down to the Prophet and what was sent down to the messengers before him. The explanation draws out why that matters here. Although the opening verses of the surah describe the believers, they carry an allusion that rebukes the unbelievers among the People of the Book. Those people claimed to hold true whatever the earlier messengers had brought, while at the same time calling the Prophet a liar and denying what he had been given. They claimed to be rightly guided all the same, and claimed that nobody would enter the Garden except a Jew or a Christian. These verses brand that claim a lie, because believing in the earlier Books cannot be separated from believing in the one sent down now.

phrases.translation: and have sure faith in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The Hereafter is an attribute belonging to the Abode, as in the verse that calls the final Abode the true Life. It is described as last only because it comes after an earlier abode that preceded it, as when a speaker says he showed someone favors one time after another and was thanked for neither the first nor the last. A second explanation is that it is called last because it comes after the creation, just as the present world is called the nearer world from its nearness to the creation. Certainty about it is knowledge of a thing that has not arrived yet, held without wavering.

phrases.translation: It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful
phrases.explanation:
The exegetes differed over whom this verse means by they. Some took it to cover the people of the two qualities mentioned before, the believers in the unseen among the Arabs and the believers in what was sent down to the Prophet and to the messengers before him, all of them described as following guidance from Allah and as the successful. Others took it to mean the God-fearing who believe in the unseen, and held that these are the same people as those who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and before him. Others again took it to mean the believers among the People of the Book, who held the Prophet and what he brought to be true and had already believed in the remaining prophets and Books.

The reading preferred here is the first. They refers to both groups together, the God-fearing and those who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet, and the second those is joined to what came before it. The grammar was worked through at length to reach that result, since the second those can stand in the genitive by two routes and in the nominative by four, including as a fresh statement opening a new verse.

Following the guidance of their Lord means that they are upon a light from their Lord, upon a proof, and upon steadiness and correctness, because Allah confirms them and grants them success in what is right. Success itself is explained as continued existence, so the successful are those whose good lasts with them rather than ending where this world ends.

phrases.translation: As for those who persist in disbelief,
phrases.explanation:
The verse opens by naming a group whose disbelief is settled, and the scholars of interpretation differed about who is meant and about whom it came down. One explanation takes it to be the Jews around Medina at the time of the Prophet, rebuked for denying his prophethood and calling him a liar even though they knew him and were aware that he was the Messenger, knowing him as they knew their own sons. Another takes it to be particular people among the disbelievers, named and known, since some of those who disbelieved did come to believe later, and the verse cannot be about every disbeliever without exception.

Disbelief here means denial. The rabbis among the Jews of Medina denied the Prophet and concealed him from the people, keeping his affair secret while they found his description in their own books, which is why Allah elsewhere speaks of those who conceal the clear proofs He sent down.

phrases.translation: it is the same
phrases.explanation: The word for the same means being in equilibrium, and it comes from the same root as the word for equality, so a speaker says these two matters are equal to me and they are the same to me with one meaning. The Quran uses it that way elsewhere when it tells the Prophet to throw a treaty back to a people on equal terms, and a poet uses it of the night and the day running level for a woman, with no slackening in either of them.

phrases.translation: whether you warn them or not—they will never believe
phrases.explanation: The two halves of the sentence are put in the form of a question but mean a statement, since the particle here stands in place of the word for which of the two. A speaker says it makes no difference to us whether you stand or sit, and asks nothing by it. Some grammarians held that the particle is simply attached to the word for the same with no question intended, because a real question seeks to settle which of two things is so, and nothing is being sought here. The sense is that warning these people and leaving them unwarned stand level, and they will not believe.

phrases.translation: Allah has sealed their hearts
phrases.explanation:
Sealing here comes from the word for impressing a stamp, and a signet is called by the same root, so to seal a document is to put a stamp upon it. Hearts are described as vessels for the knowledge entrusted to them and jars for the insights deposited in them, and hearing is what perceives sound and what lets a person come to know the truth of reports about the unseen. Sealing them is therefore comparable to sealing any other vessel or jar, and nothing is left open for what would have entered.

The exegetes differed over how that sealing is to be described. Some said the verse is only a report of their arrogance and their refusal to listen to the truth they were called to, in the way a person says that so-and-so is deaf to these words when he will not hear them and holds himself above understanding them. The view preferred here is the one a reliable narration from the Prophet supports, which takes the sealing as a real act rather than a figure for their attitude.

The argument put to the other side is direct. Their arrogance and their turning away from belief, are they their own act, or an act of Allah toward them? Whichever answer is given, what the verse describes stands. Some took the people meant here to be the leaders of the confederates who were killed at Badr.

phrases.translation: and their hearing, and their sight is covered.
phrases.explanation: The report about sealing ends at their hearing, and what follows about the eyes is a fresh statement begun after it. The proof given is that the word for covering stands in the nominative, which makes it the subject of its own sentence rather than something governed by the verb of sealing. An early exegete made the same point and supported it from the Quran, with the verse saying that if Allah wills He seals upon your heart. A covering in the speech of the Arabs is what envelops a thing entirely, as a poet used the word of something that enveloped a man and mingled with him. The reciters and the scholars agree on the reading followed here, and whoever departs from it stands alone against what they established together.

phrases.translation: They will suffer a tremendous punishment
phrases.explanation:
The punishment is mighty, and the explanation of the phrase is given as Ibn Abbas put it, that it belongs to them on account of their opposition to the Prophet, and that it concerns the scribes among the Jews. Others connected these two verses with the people who exchanged the favor of Allah for disbelief and settled their own folk in the abode of ruin, and said that of the leaders among them none responded, none was saved and none was guided.

The verse is also treated as one of the clearest proofs against those who deny that a person can be charged with what he cannot bear except by the help of Allah. Allah reported that He sealed the hearts and the hearing of a group of His unbelieving servants, and He did not lift the obligation from them or remove His commands from any of them.

phrases.translation: And there are some who say,
phrases.explanation:
Two views are recorded about the word for people itself. One takes its original form to have begun with a hamza that was dropped because the word is used so constantly, after which the definite article was added and its lam assimilated into the nun, in the way the Quran writes but as for me, He is Allah, my Lord. The other holds that it is a different form altogether, because the Arabs build its diminutive on the letters as they stand rather than restoring the dropped hamza.

The exegetes agree that this verse came down about a group given to hypocrisy and that the description is theirs. The occasion given for it is that when the Prophet's position was established in the land of his migration, and Allah's word prevailed there and Islam spread through its houses, and the Muslims overcame the idolaters and the People of the Book there were humbled, then the learned among the Jews showed the Prophet their rancour and open enmity, out of envy and insolence, except for a small group whom Allah guided and who became Muslim. Belief in what they say with their tongues means holding something to be true, which is the sense established earlier.

phrases.translation: “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not ˹true˺ believers
phrases.explanation:
A day is called a day among the Arabs only because of the night that precedes it, and without a preceding night the daylight is not called a day. The Day of Resurrection is therefore a day after which no night comes, except the night whose morning the Resurrection breaks in.

Allah then denies these people the name of belief even though He has reported what they said with their tongues. That is a flat contradiction of what they claimed about their own conviction and their acknowledgment of the Resurrection, and it tells the Prophet that what they show him with their mouths is the opposite of what lies hidden in their hearts and the reverse of what their souls are set on.

phrases.translation: They seek to deceive Allah and the believers,
phrases.explanation: The deception of the hypocrite is that he shows with his tongue words and assent contradicting the doubt and denial living in his heart, so that what he displays protects him. Some who knew the language held that the verb here, though it comes in the reciprocal pattern, carries the plain sense of deceiving rather than of trying to deceive. The view preferred is the opposite. The form belongs to the reciprocal action that only happens between two parties, as it does throughout Arabic. So the hypocrite tries to deceive Allah by the lie on his tongue, and Allah is his deceiver, in that He leaves him without sight of what would save him at his return. The respite granted to such people is only that they may increase in sin, and on the Day they will ask the believers to wait so that they may take some of their light, and a wall with a gate will be struck between them, mercy inside it and punishment outside.

phrases.translation: yet they only deceive themselves,
phrases.explanation:
Arabs do call a man a deceiver toward someone he has escaped, when he shows with his tongue something other than what is inside him and so gets away with it. On that usage the hypocrite is a deceiver of Allah and the believers, because what he displays saves him from killing, captivity and immediate punishment while he carries something else within. Yet that very act deceives himself, since he seems to give himself what it wants while in fact leading it to destruction and to a wrath it cannot bear.

It would be wrong to say they deceived the believers, since that would grant them a deception actually carried off. The comparison given is a man who fought another and killed himself but not his companion, where the fighting is affirmed, the killing of the other denied and the killing of himself affirmed. A deceiver is one whose deception succeeded, and theirs did not.

phrases.translation: but they fail to perceive it
phrases.explanation: To perceive something means to know it and recognise it. What these people do not perceive is that Allah is the one deceiving them, by the respite He gives them and the gradual way He leads them on, which they take for a good thing granted to them when it is the opposite.

phrases.translation: There is sickness in their hearts,
phrases.explanation: The disease in the heart is not an illness of the body. It sits in the conviction these people hold to in religion, and in their position toward the Prophet and what he brought from Allah. What that disease consists of is doubt about his affair and confusion over it. They are neither certain of it with the certainty that belongs to belief, nor have they come out against it openly, and the unsettled state between the two is the sickness named here. The interpreters reinforced one another in this explanation, so it is not the reading of one school only.

phrases.translation: and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase.
phrases.explanation: The increase is of the same kind as what was already there. The disease Allah reports having increased for them is the doubt and confusion in their hearts before the increase, made greater rather than replaced by something else. The means of that increase is what Allah brought into being of prescribed limits and obligations, so that every fresh command and every new revelation gave their doubt something further to fasten on, and the sickness grew by what should have cured it.

phrases.translation: They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies
phrases.explanation: Painful here means causing pain, the active sense carried by a form that looks passive, in the way Arabic speaks of a painful blow for one that causes pain. The word for the reason they are punished was read in two ways. Most of the reciters of Kufa read it as lying, while others read it as denying, holding that the punishment falls on them for calling the Prophet a liar rather than for ordinary falsehood, which would not by itself bring such a threat. The reading preferred follows the shape of the passage. These verses opened by naming the shameful deeds of the hypocrites, so the threat that closes them answers what was opened, and the punishment is tied to the falsehood they were actually practising.

phrases.translation: When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”
phrases.explanation:
Two interpretations of this verse are recorded, and the one preferred is that it came down about the hypocrites of the Prophet's own time, while still taking in everyone who carries the same trait after them until the Day of Resurrection. It is chosen because the scholars of interpretation agree that this was the character of the hypocrites among the Prophet's companions and that these verses were revealed about them, and an interpretation held by consensus beats one with nothing behind it from a principle or a parallel case.

Their claim to be reformers is then examined. Whatever their reform amounted to, whether reconciling the Jews and the Muslims or managing their own religious position while lying to the believers about what was in their hearts, they believed themselves to be doing good. In their own eyes they were doers of good, and in the sight of Allah doers of evil who went against His command, since He had obliged them to believe in His Messenger and in what he brought exactly as He obliged the believers.

phrases.translation: Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it
phrases.explanation: This verse answers their claim and gives it the lie. They were commanded to obey Allah in what He commanded and forbidden to disobey Him in what He forbade, and their reply was that they were only reformers and not corrupters, that in the very thing they were blamed for they stood on righteousness and guidance, and that they were by no means the ones astray. The correction is therefore not about what they did but about who was blind to it, since they did not perceive that the corruption was theirs.

phrases.translation: And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know
phrases.explanation:
The command is explained as an instruction to give credence to the Prophet and what he brought from Allah in the way the people have given credence to it. The people meant are the believers who accepted him and his prophethood, so the hypocrites are told to believe as those believers believed.

Their answer turns on a word worth explaining. Fools is the plural of a term for someone ignorant and weak in judgment, with little knowledge of where benefit and harm lie. The Quran uses the same plural of women and children where it forbids handing wealth over to the fools, and most exegetes explained that as weakness of judgment and slight knowledge of the interests wealth should be spent on. So the insult the hypocrites throw at the believers is the language of someone who thinks he sees consequences others cannot. The verse returns it on them. They are the fools and do not know it, and ignorance of one's own condition is what makes the foolishness complete.

phrases.translation: When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.”
phrases.explanation: In public, these people claim to share the believers’ faith. The contrast between this declaration and what they say in private reveals a deliberate double face. The verse warns against treating words alone as proof of sincerity, while its account of hypocrisy leaves ultimate judgment of individual hearts to God.

phrases.translation: But when alone with their evil associates
phrases.explanation: Away from the believers, they return to those who share their corrupt conduct and reveal what they truly intend. The phrase emphasizes the contrast between public performance and private allegiance. The passage is about the hypocrisy it describes, not an instruction to distrust people merely because they have private conversations or different companions.

phrases.translation: they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”
phrases.explanation: They assure their associates that their public claim of faith was a performance and that they were making fun of the believers. This exposes their deception as intentional. The verse criticizes ridicule and double dealing, showing how mockery can be used to hide rejection rather than engage seriously with the message.

phrases.translation: Allah will throw their mockery back at them,
phrases.explanation: The response to their mockery is that they will face its consequence from Allah. The wording conveys a fitting reversal: their attempt to belittle the believers does not give them control over the outcome. Their deception is known, and the verse warns that contemptuous behavior will not shield them from accountability.

phrases.translation: leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance
phrases.explanation: They are allowed to continue in the course they chose, moving without the clarity of guidance. “Wandering blindly” describes spiritual confusion, not physical blindness. The phrase warns that persistently mocking truth can deepen a person’s estrangement from it, until they do not recognize how far their choices have led them.

phrases.translation: They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance.
phrases.explanation: The verse pictures a deliberate exchange: they abandon guidance and choose misguidance instead. It is a loss-making bargain because they give up the way that could lead to truth and lasting good. The image connects their rejection with the earlier description of concealed belief, showing the cost of choosing deception.

phrases.translation: But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: Their exchange brings no real benefit and does not lead them to the outcome they seek. Calling it profitless underlines that worldly advantage cannot compensate for losing guidance. The verse concludes that they are not on the right path, reinforcing the contrast between apparent gain and the deeper loss of rejecting truth.

phrases.translation: Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire,
phrases.explanation: The parable begins with a person who lights a fire, suggesting a moment when light and visibility are available. The image helps readers picture guidance as illumination. It is a comparison of spiritual perception, not a claim about a specific historical event, and prepares for the sudden loss of light in the rest of the verse.

phrases.translation: but when it lights up all around them,
phrases.explanation: For a moment, the fire makes the surroundings visible. The image suggests that the hypocrites encounter signs and hear the message, yet do not remain open to its guidance. The temporary brightness matters because it makes the following darkness a loss of an opportunity they had briefly been able to see.

phrases.translation: Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see
phrases.explanation: The darkness portrays their inability to find direction after turning away from the light they encountered. It is a spiritual image of confusion and rejection, not a literal description. The parable warns that refusing guidance can leave people without the clarity they once had, unable to discern the way forward.

phrases.translation: They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺
phrases.explanation: These descriptions are figurative: they refuse to hear, speak, or see in a way that responds to truth. They do not refer to people with disabilities. The verse presents the hypocrites as unwilling to take guidance, and warns that persistent refusal makes returning to the right path unlikely.

phrases.translation: Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning.
phrases.explanation: A second parable compares the disbelievers to people caught in a storm filled with darkness, thunder, and lightning. The intense weather evokes fear and confusion. Unlike the fire image, this scene emphasizes a person overwhelmed by frightening signs, illustrating how the message can be received with anxiety rather than trust.

phrases.translation: They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death.
phrases.explanation: The people in the storm try to block out the sound because they fear it may bring death. This image conveys an attempt to avoid hearing a warning that feels threatening. It does not portray the storm as a literal event affecting a named group, but dramatizes fearful resistance to a message they find difficult.

phrases.translation: And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺
phrases.explanation: The storm does not place anyone beyond God’s power. Allah encompasses those who reject the message, meaning they cannot escape His knowledge or authority. The phrase completes the image by shifting from the storm’s danger to God’s control, reminding readers that fear and denial do not remove accountability.

phrases.translation: It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight.
phrases.explanation: The lightning is so intense that it seems ready to take away their sight. In the parable, this reflects how overwhelming the signs appear to those who fear the message. The image conveys instability: they catch glimpses of clarity, but are not securely guided and remain vulnerable to confusion.

phrases.translation: Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light,
phrases.explanation: They move forward while a flash gives temporary visibility. This represents taking advantage of brief moments of clarity without committing to guidance. The passage portrays an inconsistent response: they proceed when the message seems favorable, but do not hold firmly to it when difficulty or uncertainty returns.

phrases.translation: but when darkness covers them, they stand still.
phrases.explanation: When the light disappears, they cannot move ahead. The contrast depicts indecision and dependence on temporary conditions rather than steady faith. The parable warns that refusing a consistent commitment to truth leaves a person directionless whenever circumstances become difficult. Their stillness contrasts with the movement they make under a flash, making the loss of direction vivid.

phrases.translation: Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight.
phrases.explanation: The verse reminds the audience that hearing and sight are gifts under God’s power. In context, the storm imagery has not placed the disbelievers outside divine control. The warning calls for gratitude and reflection, rather than treating the faculties of perception as something people possess independently.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything
phrases.explanation: This conclusion affirms Allah’s complete power over creation and human perception. It reinforces the warning that people cannot escape divine authority through denial. At the same time, the preceding images invite readers to use the ability to hear and see as an opportunity to recognize guidance while it is available.

phrases.translation: O humanity!
phrases.explanation: The address widens beyond the believers to humanity as a whole. It invites every listener to consider the relationship with the Lord who created them. The verse does not begin with a tribal or social distinction, but with a shared origin and a call to worship the Creator.

phrases.translation: Worship your Lord,
phrases.explanation: Worship means directing devotion and obedience to God. Calling Allah “your Lord” recalls His care and authority over human life. The command is grounded in the relationship between Creator and creation, and it calls people to gratitude, trust, and responsible living rather than worshipping what cannot create or sustain them.

phrases.translation: Who created you and those before you,
phrases.explanation: The verse points to creation as a reason for worship. The audience and earlier generations alike depend on God for existence, so no generation is self-sufficient. This shared dependence challenges pride and reminds people that their lives are gifts, not achievements that make them independent of their Creator.

phrases.translation: so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: Mindfulness of God means awareness that shapes choices and restrains wrongdoing. Worship is meant to form a life of responsibility, not remain an empty ritual. The verse links devotion to its ethical purpose: people worship their Lord so they may live with reverence and keep His guidance in view.

phrases.translation: ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy;
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the earth as a place where people can live and the sky as a covering above them. These images direct attention to the ordered environment that sustains human life. The wording presents the world as a provision from God, inviting gratitude rather than treating creation as independent of its Maker.

phrases.translation: and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you.
phrases.explanation: Rain supports the growth of plants and fruits that sustain people. The verse links visible natural processes with divine provision, encouraging reflection on how life depends on conditions humans do not control. The fruit is described as a gift, which calls for gratitude and responsible use rather than arrogance or waste.

phrases.translation: So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺
phrases.explanation: Because Allah alone creates and provides, people should not knowingly treat another being as His equal in worship. The command connects belief with the signs just described in the earth, sky, rain, and fruit. It asks listeners to direct devotion to the source of their life and provision, not to rivals without creative power.

phrases.translation: And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant,
phrases.explanation: The challenge addresses those who question the revelation given to Muhammad. “Our servant” is an honorific description of the Prophet as a devoted recipient of God’s message. The verse treats the doubt as an invitation to test the claim, rather than relying only on assertion or mockery.

phrases.translation: then produce a sûrah like it
phrases.explanation: The listeners are challenged to produce a chapter comparable to the Qur’an. A sûrah is a chapter of the revelation. The test asks those who doubt its divine origin to meet its language and message with something like it, rather than merely claiming that it could have been composed by a human.

phrases.translation: and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true
phrases.explanation: The challenge includes gathering supporters or resources apart from God. This makes the test public and direct: if the claim of human authorship is true, the doubters may call on those who can help them. The phrase invites an honest demonstration of the claim, not an endless dispute without evidence.

phrases.translation: But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—
phrases.explanation: The verse states that the challenge will not be met. Its force lies in the contrast between the doubters’ claim and their inability to produce a comparable chapter. The wording moves from a test of the revelation to a warning about its implications if it is indeed from God.

phrases.translation: then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones,
phrases.explanation: The Fire is described as a real and grave consequence, with people and stones as its fuel. This warning calls the audience to take the challenge seriously rather than treating rejection as inconsequential. Fear here means moral caution and a reason to turn toward truth before facing the final consequence.

phrases.translation: which is prepared for the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The verse identifies the Fire as the consequence prepared for those who reject faith. It completes the warning begun by the challenge. The purpose is not to encourage people to condemn others, but to make listeners aware that rejecting divine guidance has consequences and to urge them to respond sincerely. This warning calls for taking accountability seriously.

phrases.translation: Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to bring glad tidings to people whose faith is accompanied by good deeds. Belief and action appear together, showing that faith shapes conduct. The message offers hope to those who trust God and live righteously, rather than limiting the promise to a claim made without corresponding choices.

phrases.translation: that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow.
phrases.explanation: The Gardens are described as a lasting home of delight, with rivers flowing beneath them. This image of abundance contrasts with the limits and hardships of worldly life. The promise gives believers a reason for patience and hope, while emphasizing that their ultimate reward comes from God.

phrases.translation: Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,”
phrases.explanation: The fruit will be familiar in appearance, prompting the people of Paradise to recognize a resemblance to what they knew. The comparison connects the promised reward with human experience while suggesting that its reality surpasses ordinary expectation. The verse conveys continuity and delight rather than a detailed inventory of the unseen.

phrases.translation: for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺.
phrases.explanation: The fruit resembles what they have received before, though its experience is not identical. Familiarity makes the gift recognizable, while difference suggests fresh delight. The verse uses an accessible image to communicate the joy and abundance of Paradise without claiming that the unseen can be fully captured by worldly comparisons.

phrases.translation: They will have pure spouses,
phrases.explanation: The promise includes companionship described as pure, free from the harms and impurities that affect relationships in worldly life. The wording presents the reward as dignified and joyful. It should be read as part of a broader description of Paradise, not reduced to one feature or detached from the chapter’s message of faith and good action.

phrases.translation: and they will be there forever
phrases.explanation: The final promise is permanence. Unlike worldly pleasures that end, the people described will remain in Paradise. This assurance completes the glad tidings with the security of lasting life and encourages believers to keep faith and good deeds in view beyond temporary gains. Their lasting home is part of the promise.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller.
phrases.explanation: No creature is too small to serve as an example in revelation. The verse answers objections to parables involving humble creatures: a teaching is not diminished by the size of its image. The point is whether people understand the truth it conveys, not whether the example appears grand according to human standards.

phrases.translation: As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord.
phrases.explanation: Believers recognize the parable as truthful guidance from God. Their response is to consider its meaning rather than dismiss it because of the creature used. The verse describes a receptive approach to revelation, in which even a small example can teach something important about faith and human conduct.

phrases.translation: And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?”
phrases.explanation: Those who reject faith turn the parable into an objection and ask why such an example is used. The question is presented as argumentative rather than a sincere effort to understand. The contrast shows that the same revelation can prompt reflection in some and resistance in others, depending on their response.

phrases.translation: Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many.
phrases.explanation: The parable becomes a test that reveals how people respond to guidance. Some turn away and deepen their error, while others accept its lesson and are guided. The verse does not portray God as misleading sincere seekers without cause. It emphasizes that people’s attitudes toward revelation have consequences for their direction.

phrases.translation: And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—
phrases.explanation: The verse identifies rebellion as the condition connected with straying. It introduces a description of those who break their commitments and cause harm. The passage is not saying that ordinary mistakes make someone irredeemable. It warns about persistent defiance that rejects guidance and refuses moral responsibility.

phrases.translation: those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes people who break a binding commitment to God after it has been established. A covenant implies responsibility and trust, not a casual promise. The warning concerns deliberate breach and introduces a pattern of conduct that includes breaking ties and spreading corruption. Such deliberate breaking damages trust.

phrases.translation: break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained,
phrases.explanation: These ties can include relationships and duties that God commands people to honor. Breaking them harms the bonds that hold families and communities together. The phrase links faith with care for obligations to others, showing that religious commitment cannot be separated from how people treat those around them.

phrases.translation: and spread corruption in the land.
phrases.explanation: Corruption means harmful wrongdoing that damages social and moral life. The verse associates it with breaking covenants and severing ties, rather than with mere disagreement. Its warning is about conduct that causes real harm and violates responsibilities, urging people to repair rather than undermine the order entrusted to them.

phrases.translation: It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers
phrases.explanation: The people described lose what matters most by rejecting guidance and damaging their relationships and communities. Their apparent gains cannot make up for the spiritual and moral loss. The verse concludes that success should not be measured by temporary advantage when a person abandons the commitments that lead to lasting good.

phrases.translation: How can you deny Allah?
phrases.explanation: The question challenges the audience to consider how denial can make sense in light of their own existence and dependence. It is a rhetorical invitation to reflect, not simply a request for a spoken reply. The following stages of life are given as evidence that human beings do not control their own origin or final return.

phrases.translation: You were lifeless and He gave you life,
phrases.explanation: Human beings did not bring themselves into existence. Life is presented as a gift from God, who gives being where there was none. This reminder places human life within divine power and care, and it challenges the idea that people are independent of the One who created and sustains them.

phrases.translation: then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life,
phrases.explanation: Death is not the end of the account: the verse states that God will bring people back to life. The sequence of life and death points to divine power over human existence at every stage. It grounds belief in resurrection in the same power that first gave life.

phrases.translation: and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned
phrases.explanation: The final return means that people will come before God for judgment and accountability. Life therefore has a direction and a purpose beyond its present span. The verse joins creation and resurrection to ethical responsibility, urging people to consider what they do before the One to whom they will return.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you.
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the earth’s provisions as gifts made available for human life. This is not a claim that people may use creation carelessly, but a reminder that its resources come from God and call for gratitude. The statement directs attention from created things to their Creator and provider.

phrases.translation: Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens.
phrases.explanation: The verse moves from the earth to the heavens, describing divine creation and ordering on a vast scale. The seven heavens belong to realities beyond ordinary human observation. The statement affirms God’s power over the whole cosmos, while leaving details of the unseen beyond what the verse itself explains.

phrases.translation: And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things
phrases.explanation: God’s knowledge encompasses everything He creates, seen and unseen. The conclusion connects the ordering of the cosmos with complete divine awareness. Nothing in human life or the wider universe is hidden from Him. This offers reassurance of God’s wisdom and also grounds accountability for the choices people make.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels,
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to the announcement that God made to the angels about humanity on earth. “Remember” invites the audience to reflect on this account and its meaning. The scene introduces the human role in the world while emphasizing that God’s knowledge and purpose exceed what the angels or people can fully see.

phrases.translation: “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.”
phrases.explanation: The announcement concerns a human successor or representative on earth, a being entrusted with life and responsibility in the world. The wording points to humanity’s role across generations. It does not suggest that humans own the earth absolutely, but that their position involves accountability under the Lord who placed them there.

phrases.translation: They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood
phrases.explanation: The angels ask about the possibility of human wrongdoing and violence. Their question raises the harm people may cause, but it is not presented as a challenge to God’s wisdom. The account acknowledges moral risk in human life and prepares for God’s response that His knowledge includes what they do not know.

phrases.translation: while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?”
phrases.explanation: The angels contrast possible human corruption with their own worship and reverence. Their statement describes their devotion, not a claim that worship alone makes them superior to humanity. The exchange raises a question about human purpose, setting the stage for the knowledge and capacities that God will reveal in the following verses.

phrases.translation: Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.”
phrases.explanation: God’s reply affirms that His knowledge is broader than the angels’ view of potential human wrongdoing. The verse does not give every detail of what He knows, leaving the matter open for the next part of the narrative. It invites humility before divine wisdom and caution against judging a whole purpose by only one risk.

phrases.translation: He taught Adam the names of all things,
phrases.explanation: God grants Adam knowledge by teaching him the names. The account highlights a capacity given by God, not an achievement Adam produced independently. Naming things represents knowledge that enables people to understand and communicate about the world. This detail begins to answer the angels’ question about humanity’s place and potential.

phrases.translation: then He presented them to the angels
phrases.explanation: The things whose names Adam learned are then presented to the angels. The sequence creates a test of what each knows and prepares the angels to respond. It also demonstrates that knowledge is granted by God and that different creatures may have distinct capacities within the purpose He has established.

phrases.translation: and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?”
phrases.explanation: God asks the angels to name what has been presented, in connection with their earlier question. The challenge brings the limits of their knowledge into view without portraying them as rebellious. The scene shows that judging humanity only by the possibility of wrongdoing misses capacities and purposes known fully to God.

phrases.translation: They replied, “Glory be to You!
phrases.explanation: The angels begin by declaring God’s perfection. They acknowledge that His knowledge and wisdom are beyond any flaw or limitation. Their response is reverent rather than defensive, showing that their earlier question was not a challenge to divine authority but a request for understanding. Their first words show reverence before their admission of limited knowledge.

phrases.translation: We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.
phrases.explanation: The angels admit that their knowledge is received from God and limited to what He teaches. This humility contrasts with any claim to independent or complete understanding. The verse presents learning as a gift and models honest acknowledgment of what one does not know. They do not claim knowledge beyond what has been granted to them.

phrases.translation: You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”
phrases.explanation: The angels affirm that God knows everything and acts with wisdom. The statement answers the question raised by their limited perspective: God’s decision about humanity rests on knowledge they do not possess. The verse encourages trust in divine wisdom while reminding readers not to assume their own view encompasses every consequence or purpose.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.”
phrases.explanation: God directs Adam to share the knowledge he has been taught. The command makes that knowledge visible in the gathering and demonstrates Adam’s capacity through action. The verse continues to show that God gives human beings abilities that serve a purpose, while remaining the ultimate source of what they know.

phrases.translation: Then when Adam did,
phrases.explanation: Adam carries out the instruction and names what had been presented. His response demonstrates the knowledge granted to him. The phrase is brief but marks the completion of the task before God addresses the angels, moving the narrative from the display of knowledge to its meaning.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth,
phrases.explanation: God reminds the angels that His knowledge includes what is hidden throughout creation. The statement explains why His decision cannot be judged from a limited view of possible human corruption. Divine knowledge encompasses both visible actions and realities not yet disclosed. The reminder places the earlier question within God’s complete knowledge.

phrases.translation: and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”
phrases.explanation: God’s knowledge includes both spoken words and hidden thoughts. Nothing is outside His awareness, including the angels’ question and whatever lies behind it. The verse concludes the exchange by affirming complete divine knowledge, encouraging people to be honest inwardly as well as outwardly. Both outward speech and inward realities remain known to God.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,”
phrases.explanation: The command to prostrate before Adam is an act of obedience to God’s instruction, not worship of Adam. The verse introduces a test of response to divine command. It highlights Adam’s honored place in the account while making clear that the angels’ action is directed by God.

phrases.translation: so they all did—but not Iblîs,
phrases.explanation: The angels obey, while Iblis refuses. The contrast makes his exception important: disobedience is not attributed to the angels as a group. The verse identifies a specific refusal and moves to explain its cause, showing how one being’s choice separates him from the obedient response.

phrases.translation: who refused and acted arrogantly,
phrases.explanation: Iblis refuses the command and responds with arrogance. Pride prevents him from accepting what God has instructed. The account warns that disobedience may arise not from lack of information but from a self-important refusal to submit to truth. His choice contrasts with the angels’ immediate obedience to the command.

phrases.translation: becoming unfaithful
phrases.explanation: Iblis’s refusal places him among those who reject God’s command. The phrase closes the account of his choice and its moral meaning. It emphasizes that status or knowledge does not protect someone who knowingly chooses arrogance over obedience. The account makes his deliberate disobedience a warning against pride.

phrases.translation: We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise
phrases.explanation: Adam and his wife are given a home in Paradise and permission to live there. The address begins with a caution, placing their freedom within a clear instruction. The account presents human life as involving both gifts and responsibilities, rather than unrestricted choice without guidance.

phrases.translation: and eat as freely as you please,
phrases.explanation: They are allowed broad enjoyment of the provisions in Paradise. The permission is generous and establishes that the coming prohibition concerns one specific boundary, not a general denial of good things. The verse presents divine guidance alongside abundance and freedom. Their permission is broad, with one clearly stated boundary.

phrases.translation: but do not approach this tree,
phrases.explanation: The command sets a specific limit within their permitted enjoyment. The wording warns them not to approach the tree, emphasizing caution around the boundary. The narrative does not identify the tree here, so readers should not claim details the verse does not give. The instruction marks a limit within the abundance they enjoy.

phrases.translation: or else you will be wrongdoers.”
phrases.explanation: Crossing the stated limit would be wrongdoing. The warning makes the moral consequence clear before the test occurs. The verse shows that freedom is accompanied by responsibility and that divine instruction gives people a way to distinguish permitted enjoyment from a prohibited act. The warning gives them notice of the consequence before they act.

phrases.translation: But Satan deceived them—
phrases.explanation: Satan becomes the means by which Adam and his wife are led into disobedience. The phrase names deception as the cause of their fall from the state they had enjoyed. The account warns readers about misleading persuasion and the need to remain attentive to divine guidance.

phrases.translation: leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in,
phrases.explanation: Their disobedience results in leaving the ease and happiness they had experienced. The wording links the loss to the deception that preceded it. The verse presents a serious consequence but does not make the story one of permanent hopelessness, since the following account will speak of repentance.

phrases.translation: and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other.
phrases.explanation: The command marks a transition from Paradise to earthly life and describes enmity among those involved. Human existence on earth includes conflict and moral struggle. The verse gives the setting for life after the fall, but the later promise of guidance means that people are not left without direction.

phrases.translation: You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”
phrases.explanation: Earth is designated as a place to live and receive provision for a limited time. The phrase combines the reality of worldly life with its temporal nature. People may make homes and use resources, but their stay is not permanent, so they remain accountable to God beyond this life.

phrases.translation: Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord,
phrases.explanation: After the disobedience, God guides Adam to words of repentance. The phrase shows that returning begins with help from the Lord, not with self-justification. Adam is given a way to acknowledge the wrong and seek forgiveness, establishing the possibility of repentance after failure. The prayer opens a path back after a real mistake.

phrases.translation: so He accepted his repentance.
phrases.explanation: God accepts Adam’s repentance, showing that the mistake is not beyond forgiveness when met with sincere return. The verse offers hope without minimizing the wrongdoing. Repentance includes turning back to God rather than persisting in denial, and the acceptance belongs to divine mercy. Acceptance shows that sincere return can follow wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: These names emphasize that God repeatedly accepts sincere repentance and shows mercy. They explain why Adam’s return is received and assure later readers that failure need not end in despair. The verse joins accountability with hope: people should acknowledge wrongdoing, seek forgiveness, and trust in God’s mercy.

phrases.translation: We said, “Descend all of you!
phrases.explanation: The command continues the transition to earthly life. Humanity’s life on earth will be shaped by the choices made after the initial disobedience, but God’s next words promise guidance. The verse does not leave people without a way forward or present exile as the end of their relationship with God.

phrases.translation: Then when guidance comes to you from Me,
phrases.explanation: God promises that guidance will reach people. It comes from Him, giving a reliable direction amid the uncertainty and conflict of earthly life. The phrase sets a condition for what follows: people are responsible for how they respond when divine instruction comes. The promise anticipates that people will receive direction after leaving Paradise.

phrases.translation: whoever follows it,
phrases.explanation: The promise applies to anyone who follows God’s guidance. The emphasis is on the response, not ancestry or status. Following involves accepting direction and acting upon it, making the promise accessible to people who sincerely seek the path God provides. The response to that guidance determines the promised outcome.

phrases.translation: there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.explanation: Those who follow guidance are promised safety from ultimate fear and grief. This does not mean they will never experience hardship in worldly life. It points to their final security with God, offering reassurance that faithful obedience leads to a good outcome. This assurance concerns their final standing with God, not a life without hardship.

phrases.translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs
phrases.explanation: The verse contrasts followers of guidance with people who reject faith and deny God’s signs. These signs include revelations and evidence that point toward truth. The description concerns persistent rejection, and it sets out the consequence of refusing the guidance offered in the preceding verse.

phrases.translation: will be the residents of the Fire.
phrases.explanation: The Fire is described as their final dwelling. This is a serious warning about the outcome of disbelief and denial, not an invitation for readers to assign that fate to individuals. The verse emphasizes accountability and the stakes of rejecting divine signs. The warning contrasts with the safety promised to those who follow guidance.

phrases.translation: They will be there forever.”
phrases.explanation: The verse concludes by describing the duration of that punishment as lasting. Its force is to warn the audience not to treat rejection as inconsequential. Read with the preceding promise, it presents two paths and urges people to accept guidance while they have the opportunity.

phrases.translation: O children of Israel!
phrases.explanation: The address turns to the Children of Israel, calling them as a community with a history of receiving revelation and divine favors. The verses that follow recall that history and invite a response. The historical address should not be generalized into a judgment about all people of Jewish heritage today.

phrases.translation: Remember My favours upon you.
phrases.explanation: The people are asked to recall the blessings God granted them. Remembering is meant to awaken gratitude and responsibility, not merely preserve a list of past events. The passage uses their shared history as a basis for urging faithfulness to God’s covenant. Recalling these gifts is meant to renew gratitude and faithfulness.

phrases.translation: Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine,
phrases.explanation: The covenant carries obligations between God and the people addressed. They are called to honor their commitment, with God promising to fulfill His part. The verse presents faithfulness as reciprocal responsibility, while emphasizing that people must first respond to the guidance and commitments already given.

phrases.translation: and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺
phrases.explanation: The closing command directs their reverence to God alone. Awe includes respect, consciousness of accountability, and restraint from disobedience. The word “alone” reinforces exclusive devotion. The verse gathers remembrance, covenant, and reverence as connected responses to the favors God has granted. The command calls for reverence that shapes conduct and obedience.

phrases.translation: Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures.
phrases.explanation: The address calls the people to believe in revelations that affirm the truth of earlier scripture. It presents continuity between messages from God rather than competition between them. The command asks listeners to recognize what they have received and respond faithfully, instead of rejecting confirmation because it challenges their expectations.

phrases.translation: Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain.
phrases.explanation: The warning forbids leading in rejection or exchanging revelation for a temporary worldly benefit. A fleeting gain cannot outweigh the lasting value of truth. The verse criticizes deliberate concealment or denial for advantage, and invites the audience to place fidelity to God above status, profit, or fear of losing influence.

phrases.translation: And be mindful of Me
phrases.explanation: Mindfulness means keeping God’s authority and accountability in view. This closes the address by calling the listeners to reverence that shapes what they believe and do. The reminder connects acceptance of revelation with conduct, warning against treating divine instruction as something to use only when it is convenient.

phrases.translation: Do not mix truth with falsehood
phrases.explanation: The command forbids disguising falsehood by blending it with what is true. Such mixing can mislead people who rely on those claiming knowledge. The phrase calls for honesty and clarity, especially when discussing revelation. It warns that partial truth can still deceive when it is used to hide or distort the message.

phrases.translation: or hide the truth knowingly
phrases.explanation: Knowingly concealing truth is treated as a deliberate wrong, not an innocent mistake. The phrase stresses responsibility for what one knows and communicates. Together, the commands reject both distortion and silence used to mislead, calling people to make truth clear rather than manipulate it for personal or communal advantage.

phrases.translation: Establish prayer, pay alms-tax,
phrases.explanation: The commands join regular worship with giving the prescribed alms. Establishing prayer means maintaining it as a meaningful act, while alms-tax directs wealth toward obligations and those entitled to support. The verse links devotion to God with practical responsibility, showing that worship includes both ritual commitment and care in the use of wealth.

phrases.translation: and bow down with those who bow down
phrases.explanation: Bowing with those who bow down points to joining the community in worship. The phrase emphasizes shared religious practice rather than standing apart in private devotion alone. It complements prayer and alms by describing participation with others, grounding worship in both personal commitment and communal belonging.

phrases.translation: Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture?
phrases.explanation: The verse challenges people who urge others toward goodness while neglecting it themselves. Reading scripture increases responsibility because it provides knowledge of what is right. The question is a call to self-examination, not a rejection of teaching others. It asks whether one’s own conduct reflects the guidance one recommends.

phrases.translation: Do you not understand
phrases.explanation: The closing question emphasizes the contradiction between knowledge and action. Understanding scripture should affect behavior, not remain merely recited or taught. The verse warns that failing to apply what one knows is a serious inconsistency, and it invites people to bring their practice into line with their words.

phrases.translation: And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—
phrases.explanation: Patience and prayer are presented as ways to seek God’s help through difficulty. The instruction may feel demanding to people who resist humility, but the humble can accept it with trust. The next verse describes them as those certain of meeting their Lord, linking perseverance in worship with awareness of the Hereafter.

phrases.translation: those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return
phrases.explanation: This phrase explains who the humble people are: they are confident that they will meet God and return to Him. That certainty makes patience and prayer meaningful even when they are difficult. The verse connects daily worship with final accountability and hope, encouraging believers to persevere with their ultimate destination in view.

phrases.translation: O Children of Israel!
phrases.explanation: The passage again addresses the Children of Israel as a community with a particular history of revelation and divine favor. The historical address is specific and should not be generalized into a judgment about every Jewish person today. It calls the audience to remember their history and respond with gratitude and faithfulness.

phrases.translation: Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you
phrases.explanation: Remembering God’s favors means keeping the gifts and deliverance they received in mind. The call is intended to inspire gratitude and obedience, not pride in past status. The verse uses shared memory to urge a faithful response in the present. Such recollection should lead to gratitude in daily life.

phrases.translation: and how I honoured you above the others
phrases.explanation: The statement recalls a distinction and favor granted to the people addressed in their historical setting. The honor is a responsibility to respond to revelation, not a basis for arrogance or a universal ranking of present-day communities. The passage presses the listeners to live up to the guidance they were given.

phrases.translation: Guard yourselves against the Day
phrases.explanation: The verse urges people to prepare for the Day of Judgment by living responsibly now. “Guard yourselves” means taking the warning seriously rather than assuming that another person’s status will protect them. The following clauses describe how individual accountability cannot simply be transferred or escaped.

phrases.translation: on which no soul will be of help to another.
phrases.explanation: On that Day, no person can take another’s place or bear their accountability. The wording stresses the limits of human rescue at final judgment. This does not deny that people can help one another in life, but warns that each person must respond to God’s guidance and responsibility.

phrases.translation: No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given
phrases.explanation: The verse denies that intercession, payment, or outside assistance can be assumed as an automatic escape from judgment. These are forms of protection people might expect in worldly life, but they cannot replace sincere faith and obedience. The warning is meant to prevent complacency and direct the audience toward responsibility before God.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh,
phrases.explanation: The verse recalls the deliverance of the Children of Israel from Pharaoh’s rule. It presents rescue as a divine favor that should be remembered with gratitude. The account is a specific historical reference, not a general claim about later peoples or governments. The memory anchors this appeal in a concrete past event.

phrases.translation: who afflicted you with dreadful torment,
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh’s people subjected the Israelites to severe oppression. The phrase names the cruelty they experienced and makes clear why deliverance mattered. It recalls injustice without softening it, and shows the audience that God’s favor included rescue from a powerful ruler’s abuse. It reminds the audience why deliverance was necessary.

phrases.translation: slaughtering your sons and keeping your women.
phrases.explanation: The oppression included killing sons and leaving women alive, a harsh policy that terrorized families. The verse preserves the painful detail to show the severity of the trial. This historical account should be understood in its own context and not generalized into an accusation against present-day communities.

phrases.translation: That was a severe test from your Lord
phrases.explanation: The events are described as a severe test, encompassing both oppression and deliverance. The memory calls for gratitude and reflection on how people respond under hardship and after rescue. The verse connects the historical experience to the broader responsibility to remember God and follow the guidance given.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea,
phrases.explanation: The sea is parted as part of the escape from Pharaoh’s forces. The event is presented as a sign of divine power and a means of deliverance. Remembering it reminds the audience that what seemed impossible was made possible by God, and that their survival was not simply their own achievement.

phrases.translation: rescued you,
phrases.explanation: The rescue is the central outcome of the sea crossing. The short phrase emphasizes God’s direct care for those in danger. It invites gratitude and trust, particularly when circumstances seem beyond human control. The verse credits God rather than human strength alone. It highlights their dependence on divine care.

phrases.translation: and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh’s pursuing forces are destroyed in the same event that saves the Israelites. The verse recalls a decisive end to the immediate threat, witnessed by those who were rescued. The memory underscores both divine protection and accountability for oppression, without turning the story into a license for present-day vengeance.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses,
phrases.explanation: The forty nights mark a period when Moses was away to receive revelation and instruction from God. The verse asks the Children of Israel to remember this interval because it tested their faithfulness. The specific time reference grounds the account in a shared history and leads into what the people did during his absence.

phrases.translation: then you worshipped the calf in his absence,
phrases.explanation: While Moses was away, some of the people turned to worshipping the calf. The verse presents this as a serious departure from the worship of God. The timing matters because it shows how quickly the people abandoned their commitment when their leader was not present.

phrases.translation: acting wrongfully
phrases.explanation: The phrase identifies calf worship as wrongdoing. It is not described as a harmless mistake, but as a breach of their relationship with God. The verse’s direct wording calls the audience to acknowledge the seriousness of the act and remember the danger of following visible objects instead of divine guidance.

phrases.translation: Even then We ˹still˺ forgave you
phrases.explanation: Despite the grave wrongdoing, God granted forgiveness. The word “even” underscores the contrast between the people’s failure and the mercy they received. This is a reminder of divine compassion, but it is not an excuse to take forgiveness lightly or repeat wrongdoing without repentance. The gift came despite their serious breach of trust.

phrases.translation: so perhaps you would be grateful
phrases.explanation: Forgiveness is meant to lead to gratitude, shown through recognizing God’s mercy and returning to obedience. The verse presents pardon as an opportunity for a changed response. Remembering that mercy should deepen thankfulness rather than make a person careless about the harm of wrongdoing. Gratitude should be visible in a faithful response.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture
phrases.explanation: The Scripture given to Moses is recalled as a gift of revelation and guidance. The people are asked to remember receiving it, which brings their responsibility into view. Revelation provides direction and knowledge, so possessing it calls for reflection and faithful practice rather than neglect.

phrases.translation: —the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺
phrases.explanation: The Scripture serves as a criterion for distinguishing truth from falsehood and right conduct from wrong. This makes revelation a practical guide, not merely a historical possession. Its purpose is to help people recognize the path they should follow and avoid confusion. It gives people a way to recognize the path they should follow.

phrases.translation: that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: The aim of the revelation is guidance. The phrase connects receiving scripture with responding to it, since guidance benefits those who attend to and follow it. The verse recalls a favor while also pointing to the responsibility that comes with being given divine direction. The revelation is meant to shape belief and action.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people!
phrases.explanation: Moses addresses his community with direct concern as he confronts their wrongdoing. The words “my people” express his relationship to them even while he delivers a difficult warning. The verse presents a moment of correction and repentance in the history recalled to the Children of Israel.

phrases.translation: Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf,
